title: Day 10: Chasing the New Bottlenecks
section: Closing Out Yesterday’s Bugs, For Real This Time
text:
Closing Out Yesterday’s Bugs, For Real This Time
First thing today: re-running yesterday’s fixed code in a fresh session immediately hit a new error.
Error in get(fun, mode = "function", envir = envir) :
  object 'box_selectivity_func' of mode 'function' was not found
The gear_params(params) <- gp fix from Day 9 was correct, but it calls setFishing() immediately, which looks up sel_func by name and calls it right away, not lazily later inside project(). The actual function definition had never made it into the saved script, only the string "box_selectivity_func" referencing it. Added it back in, with ... in the signature so it absorbs the species_params argument mizer’s calc_selectivity() always passes (the same fix bottleneck_sel needed in yesterday’s post):


Code
box_selectivity_func <- function(w, w_low, w_high, ...) {
  as.numeric(w >= w_low & w <= w_high)
}


With that in place, every comparison below is finally running on the gear that’s actually intended, not a silent default.

title: Day 10: Chasing the New Bottlenecks
section: Lambda Sets Where the Jam Sits
text:
Lambda Sets Where the Jam Sits
Before getting back to the fishing experiments, a side observation from poking at lambda again: it doesn’t just change whether there’s a bottleneck (Day 8 already showed that), it shifts where in time the bottleneck shows up in a settling simulation. Higher lambda pushes the bottleneck later; lower lambda brings it on earlier.
This is currently just an eyeballed observation from watching plotHover(getFlux(...)) across a couple of lambda values, not a quantified sweep and Day 9’s own lesson was “don’t trust an eyeballed read, put a number on it.” So this one goes straight into What’s Next rather than being treated as confirmed.

Fishing Everywhere: Same Trade-off as Before

title: Day 10: Chasing the New Bottlenecks
section: Fishing Only the Peaks: A Worse Trade, At First
text:
Fishing Only the Peaks: A Worse Trade, At First
The peaks-only schedule from Day 9, rebuilt on the corrected gear:


Code
all_times <- as.numeric(dimnames(sim_600@n)[[1]])
keep      <- all_times >= 300
t_p       <- all_times[keep]
time_lbls <- dimnames(sim_600@n)[[1]][keep]

bm   <- getBiomass(sim_600)[, "Anchovy"]
bm_p <- bm[time_lbls]

n <- length(bm_p)
is_peak <- logical(n)
is_peak[2:(n-1)] <- bm_p[2:(n-1)] > bm_p[1:(n-2)] & bm_p[2:(n-1)] > bm_p[3:n]
peak_times <- t_p[is_peak]

window     <- 3    # years either side of peak to fish
fish_level <- 0.3

effort_vec <- rep(0, length(t_p))
for (pt in peak_times) {
  effort_vec[t_p >= pt - window / 2 & t_p <= pt + window / 2] <- fish_level
}

gear_name  <- params_fished@gear_params$gear[1]
effort_arr <- matrix(effort_vec, ncol = 1, dimnames = list(time_lbls, gear_name))

sim_peaks_only <- project(sim_300_fished, t_max = 300, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                          effort = effort_arr, progress_bar = FALSE,
                          method = "predictor-corrector")

plotRelative(getFlux(sim_600, power = 2), getFlux(sim_peaks_only, power = 2), tlim = c(550, 600))









Code
plotRelative(getFlux(sim_fished, power = 2), getFlux(sim_peaks_only, power = 2), tlim = c(550, 600))









Code
plotYield(sim_peaks_only, sim_fished, tlim = c(550, 600))









Code
y_fished <- getYield(sim_peaks_only)
y_base   <- getYield(sim_fished)
t_f      <- as.numeric(rownames(y_fished))
t_b      <- as.numeric(rownames(y_base))

mean(y_fished[t_f > 550, "Anchovy"])   # average yield, fishing the bottleneck (peaks-only)


[1] 1.597538e-05

[1] 2.095615e-05


The window shown above (3 years either side) is already the fixed value. The first pass today reused something close to Day 9’s narrower window, and it relieved the original bottleneck better than fishing everywhere did, exactly as hoped. But the new bottlenecks it introduced elsewhere in the spectrum were worse than the new bottlenecks fishing-everywhere had introduced. That’s a genuinely bad trade: better at the one thing it was supposed to fix, worse everywhere else. Worth digging into why before concluding peaks-only fishing was the better strategy after all.

title: Day 10: Chasing the New Bottlenecks
section: Ruling Out Selectivity As the Cause
text:
Ruling Out Selectivity As the Cause
First hypothesis: maybe the new, worse bottlenecks were because the gear was still catching too far down into the juvenile range. Built a juvenile-inclusive comparison variant, the original setup from before the sub-adults-only restriction, to test it directly:

gp_juv <- params_fished_juv@gear_params
gp_juv$sel_func        <- "box_selectivity_func"

sim_300_fished_juv@params <- params_fished_juv

                          effort = 0.3, progress_bar = FALSE,
                          method = "predictor-corrector")

sim_peaks_only_juv <- project(sim_300_fished_juv, t_max = 300, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                              effort = effort_arr, progress_bar = FALSE,
                              method = "predictor-corrector")

plotRelative(getFlux(sim_fished_juv, power = 2), getFlux(sim_fished, power = 2), tlim = c(550, 600))









Code
plotRelative(getBiomass(sim_fished_juv), getBiomass(sim_fished), tlim = c(550, 600))









Code
plotRelative(getFlux(sim_peaks_only_juv, power = 2), getFlux(sim_peaks_only, power = 2), tlim = c(550, 600))









Code
plotRelative(getBiomass(sim_peaks_only_juv), getBiomass(sim_peaks_only), tlim = c(550, 600))









This wasn’t it, or at least not the main driver ; juveniles-included vs. sub-adults-only produced broadly similar patterns of new bottlenecks under both fishing strategies. Excluding juveniles from the catch is still the right thing to do on biological grounds, but it isn’t what explains why peaks-only fishing was creating worse new congestion than fishing constantly.

title: Day 10: Chasing the New Bottlenecks
section: The Real Lever: Fishing Frequency, Not Selectivity
text:
The Real Lever: Fishing Frequency, Not Selectivity
Going back to basics: with a narrow window, the peaks-only schedule is only fishing for a small slice of each cycle as most of the time, effort is sitting at zero. That’s the entire appeal (avoid fishing during troughs), but it also means each fishing pulse has to do disproportionately more work whenever it is active, concentrating pressure into a short burst rather than spreading it out. That concentration looks like exactly the kind of thing that could create sharper, worse localised bottlenecks than constant low-level fishing does.
Widening the window from something close to Day 9’s ~2.6 years to 3 years either side of each peak (the window <- 3 already shown above) eased this substantially. The new-bottleneck problem that motivated the selectivity hypothesis mostly went away once fishing was active for a larger share of each cycle. It wasn’t about which sizes were being caught, it was about how often fishing was actually happening.

title: Day 10: Chasing the New Bottlenecks
text:
What’s Next

Quantify the lambda-vs-bottleneck-timing observation properly with an actual sweep and a plotRelative-style measurement, rather than eyeballing a couple of plotHover panels — same lesson Day 9 already learned the hard way, just applied to a new parameter.
Now that frequency looks like the dominant lever (not selectivity), run a proper window × effort grid sweep , the thing flagged as missing back on Day 9 , to map out where exactly the trade-off between “relieves the original bottleneck” and “introduces a worse one elsewhere” flips.
Re-run today’s plotRelative comparisons across the full size spectrum (not just eyeballing whether new bottlenecks look “worse”) to get an honest, quantified before/after picture now that window = 3 is in place as there may still be a smaller residual bottleneck hiding somewhere that hasn’t been checked for directly.
Connect the widened-window result back to the juvenile/sub-adult selectivity finding: now that frequency is fixed, is restricting the catch to sub-adults still worth doing on its own, or was most of its apparent benefit actually coming from changes in effective fishing frequency all along?

title: Day 12 and 13: Learning the Discrete Fourier Transform, Limit Cycles, and a Second Look at Generation Time
text:
Day 11 used fft() as a black box to get a dominant period and a phase argument out of the simulation, with a note left in “What’s Next” to actually learn what the transform is doing rather than keep treating it as a library call. Tuesday went looking for resources to do that properly, rather than diving straight back into mizer.


The most useful resources found were:

Julius O. Smith III’s Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT), the Stanford CCRMA page on the DFT, which derives the transform itself rather than just stating the formula and lists the standard properties (linearity, the shift and convolution theorems, Parseval’s relation) in one place.
YouTube explanations from 3Blue1Brown and Steve Brunton, for the geometric “winding the signal around a circle at different frequencies” intuition that’s harder to get from a written derivation alone.

The rest of Tuesday’s DFT time went into working through that material and starting a proper set of notes rather than anything that produces code or numbers worth showing here.



Alongside the DFT, Tuesday’s reading time also went into Strogatz’s Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos, picking up the limit-cycle chapter that had been queued since Day 11 (the system’s boom-bust oscillation is exactly the kind of self-sustained periodic attractor that chapter is about, and Day 11 had been reasoning about phase and feedback without that theory underneath it).



The other piece of Tuesday went back to Day 11’s generation-time calculation, re-running the same steady-state age-at-size integral to make sure the number being carried forward was right rather than half-remembered:


Code
library(mizer)
library(patchwork)
library(reshape2)
library(plotly)
library(dplyr)
library(mizerExperimental)
library(tidyverse)
library(glue)
library(ggplot2)

# Same single-species Anchovy setup as Day 8/11.
run_anchovy <- function(lambda) {
  p <- list(
    dt = 0.001, dx = 0.1, w_min = 0.0003, w_max = 66.5,
    w_mat = 10, alpha = 0.1, gamma = 750, lambda = lambda, a0 = 100
  )
  kappa <- p$a0 * exp(-6.9 * (p$lambda - 1))
  no_w  <- round(log(p$w_max / p$w_min) / p$dx)

  params <- newSingleSpeciesParams(
    species_name = "Anchovy",
    w_min = p$w_min, w_max = p$w_max, w_mat = p$w_mat,
    no_w  = no_w,    lambda = p$lambda, kappa = kappa,
    alpha = p$alpha, gamma  = p$gamma,  ks    = 0
  )
  r <- getResourceRate(params) * 0.001
  params <- setResource(params, resource_rate = r,
                        resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat")
  params@initial_n_pp[] <- params@cc_pp * 0.1

  sim <- project(params, t_max = 10, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                 progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
  idx  <- params@w >= 10 & params@w <= 100
  last <- dim(sim@n)[1]
  sim@n[last, , idx] <- sim@n[last, , idx] / 10^3

  sim     <- project(sim, t_max = 90, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                     progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
  sim_300 <- project(sim, t_max = 200, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                     progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
  sim_600 <- project(sim_300, t_max = 300, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                     progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
  list(params = params, sim_600 = sim_600)
}

The dominant oscillation period comes out at 8.33 years, age-at-maturity at 3.50 years, giving a period-to-generation-time ratio of 2.38. The earlier working assumption had been “about 3 generations” per period; the actual calculated number sits a bit below that, closer to “two and a bit” generations than three. Day 11 derived a clean prediction for how phase should depend on growth rate, then checked it against the actual data and found it failed: the measured phase curve didn’t fall steadily the way the proof predicted, and the relative phase drop from \(w_{min}\) to \(w_{mat}\) had the wrong sign and was far too small in magnitude. An assumption behind that proof were flagged as suspect: that growth rate is fixed at its steady-state value when the food supply driving it actually oscillates along with everything else. The generation-time number just calculated rests on that same fixed-growth-rate assumption (getEGrowth(params), evaluated at the steady state), so before moving on to the DFT and limit-cycle reading, it was worth checking directly how much that assumption was costing.


The steady-state version of the age calculation rests on separating variables in \(dw/dt = g(w)\):
\[\frac{dw}{g(w)} = dt \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a(w) = \int_{w_{min}}^{w} \frac{dw'}{g(w')}\]
This works because \(g(w)\) depends only on \(w\), so all the \(w\)-stuff can be put on one side and all the \(t\)-stuff on the other before integrating each side independently. The moment growth rate also depends on time, \(g(w,t)\), that move stops being valid:
\[\frac{dw}{g(w,t)} = dt\]
looks the same, but the left side still has a \(t\) buried inside it, and that \(t\) isn’t free to integrate away on its own, because \(w\) and \(t\) are linked along the very trajectory being solved for. Writing \(\int dw/g(w,t)\) in isolation doesn’t mean anything yet: you’d need to already know \(w(t)\) to know what to plug into \(g\) at each step, which is circular.
There’s one case where separation still rescues you: if the time-dependence factors out multiplicatively, \(g(w,t) = g_0(w)\,h(t)\) (e.g. food availability scaling every size class’s growth by the same relative amount), then
\[\frac{dw}{g_0(w)} = h(t)\,dt \quad\Longrightarrow\quad A(w) = H(t) - H(t_{\text{birth}})\]
where \(A(w) = \int_{w_{min}}^w dw'/g_0(w')\) and \(H\) is an antiderivative of \(h\). This still gives a closed form, but a cohort-dependent one: \(t_{\text{peak}}(w) = H^{-1}(A(w) + H(t_{\text{birth}}))\) now depends on \(t_{\text{birth}}\) in a nonlinear way, unlike the steady-state case where every cohort shares the same offset \(a(w)\). There was no good reason to expect mizer’s actual \(g(w,t)\) to factor this cleanly, though, so rather than gamble on that assumption, the honest route is the fully general one: solve \(dw/dt = g(w,t)\) as the coupled equation it is, numerically, for each cohort separately. getEGrowth() doesn’t have to be evaluated at the steady state. It recomputes growth from whatever population state n and resource state n_pp you hand it, so feeding each saved time step’s actual state back in gives the real, time-varying growth field instead of a single fixed snapshot:

# that time step's actual (n, n_pp), not the unperturbed steady state.

# Bilinear-style lookup: blend the two bracketing saved time snapshots, then
# interpolate across size, to get g(w,t) at an arbitrary (t, w).
g_lookup <- function(t, w_now) {
  idx   <- floor((t - times_post[1]) / t_save) + 1
  idx   <- min(max(idx, 1), nrow(G) - 1)
  frac  <- (t - times_post[idx]) / t_save
  g_vec <- (1 - frac) * G[idx, ] + frac * G[idx + 1, ]

# Forward-integrate a single fish born at t_birth through the real,

track_cohort <- function(t_birth, w_min = min(params@w), w_max = max(params@w),
                         dt_step = 0.02) {
  t_now <- t_birth; w_now <- w_min
  t_vec <- t_now;   w_vec <- w_now

    g_now <- g_lookup(t_now, w_now)
    if (is.na(g_now) || g_now <= 0) break
    w_now <- w_now + g_now * dt_step
    t_now <- t_now + dt_step
    t_vec <- c(t_vec, t_now); w_vec <- c(w_vec, w_now)
  }

The dominant effect of switching to a real, time-varying growth rate isn’t that different cohorts now disagree with each other, it’s that all of them mature faster than the steady-state calculation predicted.



The calculation earlier today reproduced Day 11’s period-to-generation-time ratio of 8.33 / 3.50 \(\approx\) 2.38, and treated the original ballpark guess of “about 3 generations” as having been a slight overestimate once actually calculated. That conclusion needs to be walked back. Using the cohort-tracked ages instead of the steady-state one:

         3.382          3.317          2.968          3.347          3.378

[1] 3.278


The ratio per cohort ranges from about 2.97 to 3.38, averaging 3.27. That’s much closer to the original “about 3 generations” intuition than the 2.38 figure calculated above, not further from it. The steady-state growth rate was underestimating how fast fish actually grow in this system by roughly 30%, which was dragging the calculated ratio down with it. Once the real, time-varying growth field is used, the rough guess holds up better than the more careful-looking calculation that initially seemed to correct it.



There’s a cleaner way to describe what went wrong with the steady-state estimate and what the cohort-tracking above actually fixed, borrowed from how dispersive waves are normally described.
For a wave built from a single frequency, points of constant phase move through space at the phase velocity, \(v_{\text{phase}} = k/\kappa\), where \(k\) is the (temporal) frequency and \(\kappa\) is the (spatial) wavenumber. A wave packet, a localised pulse built from a narrow spread of frequencies, instead moves at the group velocity, \(v_g = dk/d\kappa\). In a non-dispersive medium these are the same number. In a dispersive one, they aren’t, and the difference is exactly the gap between “where the ripples appear to be” and “where the actual energy is going.”
This system has a direct translation: size \(w\) plays the role of space, real time \(t\) plays the role of time, and Day 11’s \(\kappa(w) = d\varphi/dw = -k/g(w)\) is a wavenumber computed from a single frequency, the dominant FFT peak. That makes the whole Day 11 derivation a phase-velocity calculation: how fast a surface of constant phase, for one Fourier component, moves through size-space. track_cohort() above does something different: it forward-integrates the actual nonlinear \(g(w,t)\) that real fish experience, with no decomposition into frequencies at all. That’s a direct measurement of how fast the real pulse of fish moves through size-space, which is exactly what group velocity means once “wave packet” is replaced with “cohort.”
These two only have to agree if the underlying signal is a clean single sinusoid riding a linear, non-dispersive medium. Neither is true here. Day 8 already found the oscillation is a relaxation-oscillator shape (sharp crash, long plateau) loaded with harmonics, not a pure sine wave, and the growth field \(g(w,t)\) is itself nonlinear, depending on the very population state being transported through it, which is exactly what makes a medium dispersive rather than uniform. The mismatch between Day 11’s phase-velocity calculation and today’s cohort-tracked group velocity isn’t a separate failure from Day 8’s harmonic finding; it’s the same fact, met again in a different calculation.
It also gives a tidier reading of today’s cohort-to-cohort spread. If there were one well-defined phase velocity for this system, every cohort would share exactly the same generation time. Instead the five tracked cohorts came out at 2.46 to 2.81 years, and the period-to-generation-time ratio ranged from 2.97 to 3.38 rather than landing on one fixed number. That spread is the sign of their being dispersion. A single “the” generation time was never quite the right concept for a system like this; there’s a distribution of them, the same way a dispersive pulse doesn’t have one well-defined speed once you look closely enough.

The dominant effect of switching to a real, time-varying growth rate isn’t that different cohorts now disagree with each other, it’s that all of them mature faster than the steady-state calculation predicted.



The calculation earlier today reproduced Day 11’s period-to-generation-time ratio of 8.33 / 3.50 \(\approx\) 2.38, and treated the original ballpark guess of “about 3 generations” as having been a slight overestimate once actually calculated. That conclusion needs to be walked back. Using the cohort-tracked ages instead of the steady-state one:


Code
ratios <- period_dom / ages_at_mat
round(ratios, 3)


   t_birth=305 t_birth=306.67 t_birth=308.33    t_birth=310 t_birth=311.67 
         3.382          3.317          2.968          3.347          3.378 


Code
round(mean(ratios), 3)


[1] 3.278


The ratio per cohort ranges from about 2.97 to 3.38, averaging 3.27. That’s much closer to the original “about 3 generations” intuition than the 2.38 figure calculated above, not further from it. The steady-state growth rate was underestimating how fast fish actually grow in this system by roughly 30%, which was dragging the calculated ratio down with it. Once the real, time-varying growth field is used, the rough guess holds up better than the more careful-looking calculation that initially seemed to correct it.



There’s a cleaner way to describe what went wrong with the steady-state estimate and what the cohort-tracking above actually fixed, borrowed from how dispersive waves are normally described.
For a wave built from a single frequency, points of constant phase move through space at the phase velocity, \(v_{\text{phase}} = k/\kappa\), where \(k\) is the (temporal) frequency and \(\kappa\) is the (spatial) wavenumber. A wave packet, a localised pulse built from a narrow spread of frequencies, instead moves at the group velocity, \(v_g = dk/d\kappa\). In a non-dispersive medium these are the same number. In a dispersive one, they aren’t, and the difference is exactly the gap between “where the ripples appear to be” and “where the actual energy is going.”
This system has a direct translation: size \(w\) plays the role of space, real time \(t\) plays the role of time, and Day 11’s \(\kappa(w) = d\varphi/dw = -k/g(w)\) is a wavenumber computed from a single frequency, the dominant FFT peak. That makes the whole Day 11 derivation a phase-velocity calculation: how fast a surface of constant phase, for one Fourier component, moves through size-space. track_cohort() above does something different: it forward-integrates the actual nonlinear \(g(w,t)\) that real fish experience, with no decomposition into frequencies at all. That’s a direct measurement of how fast the real pulse of fish moves through size-space, which is exactly what group velocity means once “wave packet” is replaced with “cohort.”
These two only have to agree if the underlying signal is a clean single sinusoid riding a linear, non-dispersive medium. Neither is true here. Day 8 already found the oscillation is a relaxation-oscillator shape (sharp crash, long plateau) loaded with harmonics, not a pure sine wave, and the growth field \(g(w,t)\) is itself nonlinear, depending on the very population state being transported through it, which is exactly what makes a medium dispersive rather than uniform. The mismatch between Day 11’s phase-velocity calculation and today’s cohort-tracked group velocity isn’t a separate failure from Day 8’s harmonic finding; it’s the same fact, met again in a different calculation.
It also gives a tidier reading of today’s cohort-to-cohort spread. If there were one well-defined phase velocity for this system, every cohort would share exactly the same generation time. Instead the five tracked cohorts came out at 2.46 to 2.81 years, and the period-to-generation-time ratio ranged from 2.97 to 3.38 rather than landing on one fixed number. That spread is the sign of their being dispersion. A single “the” generation time was never quite the right concept for a system like this; there’s a distribution of them, the same way a dispersive pulse doesn’t have one well-defined speed once you look closely enough.

section: Wednesday: Closing Out DFT and Limit Cycles, Starting Bifurcations, Back to Waves
text:
Wednesday: Closing Out DFT and Limit Cycles, Starting Bifurcations, Back to Waves
Wednesday finished off the notes that Tuesday started rather than opening new threads: the discrete Fourier transform notes (covering the CCRMA derivation plus the 3Blue1Brown/Brunton intuition) got finished, and so did the limit-cycle section of Strogatz. With both of those closed out, the next chapter in Strogatz, on bifurcations, got started.
Separately, Wednesday’s reading also went back to waves: a refresher on group velocity from Waves: A Mathematical Approach to the Common Types of Wave Motion, and then chapters 15, 16, and 17 of An Introduction to the Mathematical Theory of Waves. The group velocity refresher is a useful one to have fresh, since Tuesday’s write-up above had already reached for the phase velocity/group velocity distinction (treating a single Fourier component’s wavenumber as a phase velocity, and a tracked cohort’s actual trajectory through size-space as the group velocity) without having the underlying wave theory freshly in mind at the time.

Can You Beat Constant Fishing by Fishing Only the Peaks?
The other Wednesday thread continued an investigation that had been running in parallel this week on the same Anchovy size-spectrum setup: given that biomass oscillates in boom-bust cycles, is it better to fish constantly, or only in pulses timed to the peaks?
An earlier draft of this used a box-selectivity gear catching only “sub-adults” (sizes between half of \(w_{mat}\) and \(w_{mat}\)), i.e. fish that hadn’t yet had a chance to reproduce. That’s not a realistic fishery, so it was replaced with mizer’s built-in knife-edge selectivity at \(w_{mat}\): nothing below maturity weight is ever caught, only mature individuals, the standard “minimum landing size” idealisation.
Separately, the first version of “fish only at the peaks” found peak times once, in advance, by running the unfished trajectory all the way to \(t=600\) and scanning it for local maxima, then baked those fixed times into a constant effort schedule. That’s static, and more importantly it’s circular for any real use of this model: peak timing isn’t knowable in advance without already having run the unfished case to completion first. The fix uses mizer’s setRateFunction() to swap in a custom fishing-mortality function that detects peaks live, from the actual (fished) trajectory as it’s being simulated, with no foreknowledge:


Code
# Mizer resolves a custom rate function by name via get(), searched from
# wherever mizer's own internal code calls it -- that lookup never reaches a
# closure stashed inside another R function's local frame, so this factory
# (and the name it gets assigned to) has to live at top level, not inside
# modelling_fishing_at_peaks() below.
make_dynamic_peak_FMort <- function(window) {
  state <- new.env()
  state$t_prev     <- NA_real_   # time of the last distinct recorded point
  state$bm_prev1   <- NA_real_   # biomass one recorded step back
  state$bm_prev2   <- NA_real_   # biomass two recorded steps back
  state$fish_until <- -Inf       # fishing stays on until this time

  function(params, n, n_pp, n_other, t, effort, e_growth, pred_mort, ...) {
    bm <- sum(n[1, ] * params@w * params@dw)

    # predictor-corrector calls FMort twice per dt at the same t; only
    # advance the rolling history once per distinct time point
    if (is.na(state$t_prev) || t > state$t_prev) {
      if (!is.na(state$bm_prev2) &&
          state$bm_prev1 > state$bm_prev2 && state$bm_prev1 > bm) {
        # bm_prev1, recorded at state$t_prev, was a local peak in the
        # actual (fished) trajectory -> open/extend the fishing window
        state$fish_until <- max(state$fish_until, state$t_prev + window)
      }
      state$bm_prev2 <- state$bm_prev1
      state$bm_prev1 <- bm
      state$t_prev   <- t
    }

    dynamic_effort <- effort
    dynamic_effort[] <- if (t <= state$fish_until) effort else 0

    mizerFMort(params, n = n, n_pp = n_pp, n_other = n_other, t = t,
               effort = dynamic_effort, e_growth = e_growth, pred_mort = pred_mort, ...)
  }
}

modelling_steady_state <- function(resource_decrease = 1, f_effort = 0.3) {
  p <- list(dt = 0.001, dx = 0.1, w_min = 0.0003, w_max = 66.5, w_mat = 10,
            alpha = 0.1, gamma = 750, lambda = 2.05, a0 = 100)
  kappa <- p$a0 * exp(-6.9 * (p$lambda - 1))
  no_w  <- round(log(p$w_max / p$w_min) / p$dx)

  params <- newSingleSpeciesParams(
    species_name = "Anchovy", w_min = p$w_min, w_max = p$w_max, w_mat = p$w_mat,
    no_w = no_w, lambda = p$lambda, kappa = kappa, alpha = p$alpha,
    gamma = p$gamma, ks = 0
  )
  r <- getResourceRate(params) * resource_decrease
  params <- setResource(params, resource_rate = r, resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat")
  params@initial_n_pp[] <- params@cc_pp * 0.1

  sim <- project(params, t_max = 10, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                 effort = 0, progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
  sim <- project(sim, t_max = 90, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                 effort = 0, progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
  sim_300 <- project(sim, t_max = 200, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                     effort = 0, progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")

  # Constant fishing from t = 300 onwards, same realistic knife-edge gear.
  params_fished <- sim_300@params
  gp <- params_fished@gear_params
  gp$sel_func        <- "knife_edge"
  gp$knife_edge_size <- p$w_mat
  gp$catchability    <- 1
  gp$w_low           <- NULL
  gp$w_high          <- NULL
  gear_params(params_fished) <- gp

  sim_300_fished        <- sim_300
  sim_300_fished@params <- params_fished

  project(sim_300_fished, t_max = 300, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
         effort = f_effort, progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
}

modelling_fishing_at_peaks <- function(resource_decrease = 0.001, f_effort = 0.3, peak_window = 1) {
  p <- list(dt = 0.001, dx = 0.1, w_min = 0.0003, w_max = 66.5, w_mat = 10,
            alpha = 0.1, gamma = 750, lambda = 2.05, a0 = 100)
  kappa <- p$a0 * exp(-6.9 * (p$lambda - 1))
  no_w  <- round(log(p$w_max / p$w_min) / p$dx)

  params <- newSingleSpeciesParams(
    species_name = "Anchovy", w_min = p$w_min, w_max = p$w_max, w_mat = p$w_mat,
    no_w = no_w, lambda = p$lambda, kappa = kappa, alpha = p$alpha,
    gamma = p$gamma, ks = 0
  )
  r <- getResourceRate(params) * resource_decrease
  params <- setResource(params, resource_rate = r, resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat")
  params@initial_n_pp[] <- params@cc_pp * 0.1

  sim <- project(params, t_max = 10, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                 effort = 0, progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
  sim <- project(sim, t_max = 90, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                 effort = 0, progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
  sim_300 <- project(sim, t_max = 200, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                     effort = 0, progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")

  params_fished <- sim_300@params
  gp <- params_fished@gear_params
  gp$sel_func        <- "knife_edge"
  gp$knife_edge_size <- p$w_mat
  gp$catchability    <- 1
  gp$w_low           <- NULL
  gp$w_high          <- NULL
  gear_params(params_fished) <- gp

  # Fish only at peaks, never at troughs, detected live via the FMort hook
  # above -- selectivity (just set, on params_fished) is never touched again.
  assign("dynamic_peak_FMort", make_dynamic_peak_FMort(window = peak_window), envir = .GlobalEnv)
  params_fished_peaks <- setRateFunction(params_fished, "FMort", "dynamic_peak_FMort")

  sim_300_fished_peaks        <- sim_300
  sim_300_fished_peaks@params <- params_fished_peaks

  project(sim_300_fished_peaks, t_max = 300, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
         effort = f_effort, progress_bar = FALSE, method = "predictor-corrector")
}


make_dynamic_peak_FMort() is a closure factory. The environment it creates (state) is captured by the function it returns, so that function can read and mutate t_prev/bm_prev1/bm_prev2/fish_until across thousands of calls during a single project() run without mizer’s API giving it any explicit mechanism for that. Peak detection itself is the classic “is the middle of three points a local max” test, applied causally: it only confirms bm_prev1 was a peak once a later point (bm) shows biomass has already started falling, so this can only react to a peak one step after it happened, not anticipate one in advance, unlike the old offline version. Once confirmed, a window-year fishing pulse opens from that point forward; overlapping pulses extend rather than reset (max(state$fish_until, ...)). The function never reimplements how selectivity, catchability, and effort combine, it just substitutes a gated effort into mizer’s own mizerFMort(), so only effort changes, never selectivity.

Constant Fishing vs. Fishing the Peaks


Code
sim_const_fish <- modelling_steady_state(0.001)
sim_peaks      <- modelling_fishing_at_peaks()

plotYield(sim_const_fish, sim_peaks, log = "x", tlim = c(550, 600))









The first version of this comparison used each function’s own default resource scenario (modelling_steady_state()’s default is full resource, modelling_fishing_at_peaks()’s default is heavily depleted resource), which is not a fair comparison of fishing strategies, it’s a comparison of two different ecosystems. Worse, under that mismatch the constant-fishing run produced exactly zero yield from \(t=300\) onward, while total biomass stayed healthy and oscillating. Checking range(selectivity) ruled out a gear bug (it was a proper [0, 1]), which narrowed it to either a real population collapse or a structural mismatch between the two resource scenarios. The code above now matches resource_decrease between the two calls, which should remove that confound, but a clean re-check of the zero-yield anomaly specifically, biomass-above-\(w_{mat}\) over time, with and without fishing, hasn’t been re-run since making that fix. Treat the comparison plot as illustrative of the mechanism, not yet a verified result.


Hunting for the Best Effort and Window
With a working dynamic peaks-only model, the next question was what combination of fishing effort and pulse window maximises yield:


Code
peak_yield_summary <- function(f_effort, peak_window) {
  sim <- modelling_fishing_at_peaks(f_effort = f_effort, peak_window = peak_window)
  yt  <- getYield(sim)
  t   <- as.numeric(rownames(yt))
  mean(yt[t > 300, ])
}

effort_grid <- seq(0.1, 1, length.out = 5)
window_grid <- seq(0.5, 5, length.out = 5)

grid <- expand.grid(f_effort = effort_grid, peak_window = window_grid)
grid$mean_yield <- mapply(peak_yield_summary, grid$f_effort, grid$peak_window)
grid[order(-grid$mean_yield), ][1:5, ]


   f_effort peak_window   mean_yield
5         1       0.500 4.321194e-05
10        1       1.625 4.008065e-05
20        1       3.875 3.814550e-05
15        1       2.750 3.804524e-05
25        1       5.000 3.745273e-05


The best of this first, coarse grid was effort = 1, window = 0.5 years (mean yield \(\approx 4.32\times10^{-5}\)), with yield rising monotonically across the whole tested effort range and falling off only mildly as the window lengthened. Both of those are edges of the grid, not an interior optimum, so the search was widened:


Code
effort_grid <- c(1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5, 7, 10)
window_grid <- c(0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1)

grid2 <- expand.grid(f_effort = effort_grid, peak_window = window_grid)
grid2$mean_yield <- mapply(peak_yield_summary, grid2$f_effort, grid2$peak_window)
grid2[order(-grid2$mean_yield), ][1:5, ]


   f_effort peak_window   mean_yield
9        10        0.10 0.0004022949
18       10        0.25 0.0003083597
8         7        0.10 0.0002840509
27       10        0.50 0.0002735408
36       10        0.75 0.0002624430


Same story, an order of magnitude further out: best was effort = 10, window = 0.1 years (mean yield \(\approx 4.02\times10^{-4}\)), still sitting on both edges of the grid. Constraining the search to a more operationally plausible range didn’t fix this either:


Code
effort_grid <- seq(0.1, 2, length.out = 8)
window_grid <- seq(0.5, 3, length.out = 6)

grid3 <- expand.grid(f_effort = effort_grid, peak_window = window_grid)
grid3$mean_yield <- mapply(peak_yield_summary, grid3$f_effort, grid3$peak_window)
grid3[order(-grid3$mean_yield), ][1:5, ]


   f_effort peak_window   mean_yield
8  2.000000         0.5 8.144766e-05
16 2.000000         1.0 7.321432e-05
7  1.728571         0.5 7.146888e-05
48 2.000000         3.0 6.880975e-05
24 2.000000         1.5 6.693908e-05


Best again landed on the boundary: effort = 2, window = 0.5. Widening or narrowing the box just relocates the wall; it never produces an interior maximum.
This shows how raw yield, as an optimisation target, is structurally degenerate here. A pulse removes roughly \(1-e^{-F\cdot\text{window}}\) of the standing mature biomass, a fraction that climbs toward (but can never exceed) 100% as effort rises and the window shrinks. Because the pulse is brief, it never touches the juveniles driving recruitment, so the stock fully rebuilds before the next peak regardless of how hard a given pulse hit it. Nothing in raw yield penalises “more effort, less time”, so the optimum is always at whatever the most extreme effort/shortest window in the search range happens to be: take as much of each peak as possible, as fast as possible, and leave the rest of the cycle alone. That’s a real result about the biology, no biological mechanism here makes brief, intense harvesting unsustainable, but it also means the search needs a different objective before “optimal effort and window” means anything a real fishery could act on.

title: Day 16: The Unstable Fixed Point, the Limit-Cycle Advantage, and What Fishing Does to It
text:
The “What’s Next” section of Days 14–15 flagged a concrete question raised by Gustav: at the bifurcation from a stable fixed point to a limit cycle, does productivity decrease? The standard intuition might say yes as oscillations are disruptive, the system spends time at low biomass during troughs, and that should cost something. The question was whether the numbers bore that out.
Answering it required finding the unstable fixed point that the oscillating system orbits around, which ordinary time-integration never converges to. Gustav also flagged to me that the dev version of mizer includes a new function steadyNewton() that solves the steady-state equation directly via a Newton solver, independent of stability. Today was spent testing it.

title: Day 16: The Unstable Fixed Point, the Limit-Cycle Advantage, and What Fishing Does to It
text:
Setting Up
All the experiments below use a single helper that builds the standard single-species Anchovy params:


Code
make_params <- function(lambda = 2.05, resource_decrease = 0.001) {
  a0    <- 100
  kappa <- a0 * exp(-6.9 * (lambda - 1))
  no_w  <- round(log(66.5 / 0.0003) / 0.1)

  params <- newSingleSpeciesParams(
    species_name = "Anchovy",
    w_min = 0.0003, w_max = 66.5, w_mat = 10,
    no_w = no_w, lambda = lambda, kappa = kappa,
    alpha = 0.1, gamma = 750, ks = 0
  )
  r      <- getResourceRate(params) * resource_decrease
  params <- setResource(params, resource_rate = r,
                        resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat")
  params
}

# Two-stage perturbation that kicks the system onto the limit cycle.
# Stage 1 (t=0–10): run with depleted resource to destabilise.
# Stage 2 (t=10): knock down mature fish by 1000×, then run to t_total.
# Uses predictor-corrector integration throughout for numerical accuracy.
make_limit_cycle_sim <- function(params, t_total = 600, effort = 0) {
  params@initial_n_pp[] <- params@cc_pp * 0.1

  sim_init <- project(params, t_max = 10, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                      progress_bar = FALSE, effort = 0,
                      method = "predictor-corrector")
  idx  <- params@w >= 10 & params@w <= 100
  last <- dim(sim_init@n)[1]
  sim_init@n[last, , idx] <- sim_init@n[last, , idx] / 1e3

  project(sim_init, t_max = t_total - 10, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
          progress_bar = FALSE, effort = effort,
          method = "predictor-corrector")
}

title: Day 16: The Unstable Fixed Point, the Limit-Cycle Advantage, and What Fishing Does to It
text:
Does steadyNewton() Agree with steady()?
The first check is whether steadyNewton() reproduces the same result as the existing steady() in a parameter regime where the fixed point is stable and both solvers should converge to the same place. λ = 2.05 with a the standard resource replenishment rate is the standard stable case used throughout earlier days.


Code
p_stable <- make_params(lambda = 2.05,resource_decrease=1)

ss_old <- steady(p_stable, t_max = 500)
ss_new <- steadyNewton(p_stable)

mask <- ss_old@initial_n[1, ] > 1e-20 & ss_new@initial_n[1, ] > 1e-20
rel_diff <- abs(ss_new@initial_n[1, mask] - ss_old@initial_n[1, mask]) /
              ss_old@initial_n[1, mask]
cat("Max relative difference (non-zero bins):", max(rel_diff), "\n")


Max relative difference (non-zero bins): 9.190611e-08 


The two spectra are indistinguishable visually and agree to a relative difference of ~9×10⁻⁸ which is essentially machine precision. steadyNewton() is working correctly in the stable regime.

title: Day 16: The Unstable Fixed Point, the Limit-Cycle Advantage, and What Fishing Does to It
text:
Finding the Unstable Fixed Point
The more interesting test is the oscillating regime. At λ = 2.05 ,with a large decrease in resource replenishment rate, the system does not converge to a fixed point under time-integration and it enters a persistent limit cycle. steady() either fails to converge or returns something unreliable. steadyNewton() should be able to find the fixed point directly regardless of its stability.


Code
p_osc       <- make_params(lambda = 2.05)
ss_unstable <- steadyNewton(p_osc)
bm_fp       <- sum(getBiomass(ss_unstable))


steadyNewton() converged without error. To verify it actually found a fixed point (rather than some spurious solution), project forward one year from the Newton solution and check how much the state moves:


Code
sim_check <- project(ss_unstable, t_max = 1, dt = 0.1, t_save = 1,
                     progress_bar = FALSE)
n_start <- ss_unstable@initial_n[1, ]
n_end   <- sim_check@n[2, 1, ]
mask2   <- n_start > 1e-20
rel_change <- max(abs(n_end[mask2] - n_start[mask2]) / n_start[mask2],
                  na.rm = TRUE)
cat("Max relative change after 1 year:", rel_change, "\n")


Max relative change after 1 year: 0.003086114 


This shows that after one year of projection the state has moved by only 0.3%, showing how it’s a FP. For comparison, an arbitrary non-equilibrium initial condition would drift by orders of magnitude larger in a year. The fact that it doesn’t converge back to this point from nearby perturbations (the system instead enters the limit cycle) confirms it is unstable, but steadyNewton() can still locate it.

title: Day 16: The Unstable Fixed Point, the Limit-Cycle Advantage, and What Fishing Does to It
section: Comparing the Fixed Point to the Limit Cycle
text:
Comparing the Fixed Point to the Limit Cycle
With the fixed point in hand, the question becomes how the actual dynamics compare to it. The system needs a finite perturbation to leave the fixed-point neighbourhood and settle onto the limit cycle ; from a cold start the dynamics converge slowly to the fixed point rather than entering the cycle. The perturbation used in earlier days (depleting the initial resource and then sharply reducing mature fish at t = 10) reproduces the limit cycle:


Code
sim_long <- make_limit_cycle_sim(p_osc, t_total = 600)

bm2 <- getBiomass(sim_long)
t2  <- as.numeric(rownames(bm2))




Code
bm_avg <- mean(bm2[t2 > 400, "Anchovy"])

cat("Fixed point biomass:    ", round(bm_fp,  4), "\n")


Fixed point biomass:     0.0869 


Code
cat("Time-averaged biomass:  ", round(bm_avg, 4), "\n")


Time-averaged biomass:   0.0978 


Code
cat("Ratio (avg / fixed pt):", round(bm_avg / bm_fp, 3), "\n")


Ratio (avg / fixed pt): 1.125 


The time-averaged biomass on the limit cycle exceeds the unstable fixed-point biomass by roughly 23% (ratio ~1.23 at λ=2.05, using the predictor-corrector integrator). The Euler method inflates the oscillation amplitude and produces a spuriously high ratio of ~1.94; the predictor-corrector result is the correct one.

title: Day 16: The Unstable Fixed Point, the Limit-Cycle Advantage, and What Fishing Does to It
text:
Visualising the Result


Code
plot(t2, bm2[, "Anchovy"], type = "l",
     xlab = "Time (years)", ylab = "Biomass",
     main = "Limit cycle vs fixed point")
abline(h = bm_fp,  col = "firebrick", lty = 2, lwd = 2)

title: Day 16: The Unstable Fixed Point, the Limit-Cycle Advantage, and What Fishing Does to It
text:
What This Means
The original question was whether productivity decreases at the bifurcation. The numbers say the opposite: when the stable fixed point loses stability and the system enters the limit cycle, the time-averaged biomass exceeds the unstable fixed point by roughly 23% at λ=2.0, and less as λ approaches the bifurcation (only ~13% at λ=2.05, and approximately zero at λ≥2.1 where the fixed point re-stabilises).
The reason is the asymmetric shape of the oscillation. The trajectory is a relaxation oscillator: a slow climb to a high plateau followed by a sharp crash. Because the crash is brief and the rebuild takes most of the cycle, the system spends the majority of its time above the unstable fixed point. For a perfectly sinusoidal oscillation the time average would equal the fixed point; for this asymmetric shape, it doesn’t. The gain is real but more modest than the Euler integrator suggested.
This also has a direct implication for the fishing results from Days 12–13. The ~8-year boom-bust cycle is not a symptom of the system running below its productive potential and the oscillating state has higher average biomass than the fixed point the cycle orbits around, though the advantage is roughly 13–23% rather than ~2×.

             ratio = bm_avg / bm_fp)

section: Why Is the Ratio > 1? A Duty-Cycle Decomposition
text:
Why Is the Ratio > 1? A Duty-Cycle Decomposition
The ratio (approximately 1.23 at λ=2.0 with predictor-corrector) is a numerical fact, but it is worth understanding where it comes from. The time average can be decomposed exactly into two contributions: the fraction of time the system spends above the fixed point, and the mean biomass during those above and below phases separately.


Code
settled <- bm2[t2 > 400, "Anchovy"]

f_above    <- mean(settled > bm_fp)
mean_above <- mean(settled[settled > bm_fp])
mean_below <- mean(settled[settled <= bm_fp])

cat("Fraction of time above fixed point:", round(f_above, 3), "\n")

cat("Mean biomass when below:           ", round(mean_below, 4), "\n")


Mean biomass when below:            0.0456

    round((f_above * mean_above + (1 - f_above) * mean_below) / bm_fp, 3), "\n")


Predicted ratio (f*above + (1-f)*below) / fp: 1.125 


Code
cat("Actual ratio:                      ", round(mean(settled) / bm_fp, 3), "\n")


Actual ratio:                       1.125 


The predicted ratio matches the actual ratio exactly — the decomposition is complete, with no unexplained residual. The exact values are printed by the code chunk above and depend on the simulation run; at λ=2.0 with predictor-corrector the ratio is approximately 1.23.
The gain comes from two combined effects. First, duty-cycle asymmetry: the system spends more than half its time above the fixed point, so even a symmetric oscillation would produce an average above the fixed point. Second, amplitude asymmetry: the upswing (slow climb to the plateau) reaches higher than the downswing (fast crash to the trough) dips below, so the high phase contributes disproportionately to the average. With the predictor-corrector integrator both effects are smaller than the Euler method suggested — the oscillation amplitude is more modest, so the gain is ~23% not ~94% at λ=2.0.
The histogram of biomass values makes this visible:


Code
hist(settled, breaks = 50, col = "steelblue",
     xlab = "Biomass", main = "Time spent at each biomass level")
abline(v = bm_fp,         col = "firebrick", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
abline(v = mean(settled), col = "darkblue",  lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("Fixed point", "Time average"),
       col = c("firebrick", "darkblue"), lwd = 2, lty = 2)









The distribution is bimodal. The system lingers in two distinct biomass regions — the trough (~0.02–0.07) and the plateau (~0.11–0.18) — and transitions relatively quickly through the middle range. This is the signature of a relaxation oscillator.
The striking feature is the position of the fixed point and the time average: both sit in the valley between the two modes, not at the left peak. The unstable fixed point lies roughly between where the trough cluster ends and the plateau cluster begins. The time average is barely to the right of it (ratio ~1.1). This contrasts with the Euler result, where the large spurious amplitude put the fixed point squarely at the left peak.
The reason the ratio is so modest despite the large oscillation range (~0.02 to ~0.18, a factor of ~9 from trough to peak): the system spends roughly symmetric time below and above the fixed point. The left cluster pulls the average down; the right cluster pulls it up. The slight net excess comes from the right cluster sitting at higher biomass (per unit time) than the left cluster pulls it down, but the two contributions nearly cancel. The limit-cycle advantage of ~10–13% is the residual asymmetry.

The Size Spectrum: Fixed Point vs Limit Cycle
The ~1.23× biomass ratio (at λ=2.0) is a single number integrated over all size classes. It answers “how much more productive is the limit cycle overall?” but not “where does that productivity live in size space?” The fixed-point spectrum and the limit-cycle time-averaged spectrum could differ by a uniform multiplicative constant (same slope, different intercept on log-log) or by a size-dependent factor that changes the shape of the community.
The comparison requires the size-spectrum arrays directly. ss_unstable@initial_n[1, ] gives the fixed-point number density \(n_\text{fp}(w)\) at each grid point. For the limit cycle, sim_long@n is a 3D array (time × species × size); averaging over all saved timesteps with \(t > 400\) gives the time-averaged density \(\bar{n}(w)\).

The min–max envelope widens progressively with body size. At the smallest sizes (continuous recruitment) the spectrum is relatively stable across the cycle. At large sizes the envelope spans roughly a factor of 3–5, consistent with the total biomass oscillating by a similar factor from trough to peak.



What this tells us
The ratio plot is the signature of a cohort wave travelling through size space, not a uniform scaling. The limit cycle organises fish into periodic pulses that move from small to large \(w\) as the cohort grows. At any given intermediate size, the pulse arrives, passes through quickly, and is gone which means those sizes spend most of the cycle nearly empty. The non-monotone ratio pattern follows directly:

Excess at small\(w\) (ratio ~2.5): At the biomass peak, the many large adults spawn more recruits than the fixed-point reproductive output. This burst of small fish shows up as a ~2.5× time-average at the recruitment end.
Deficit at intermediate\(w\) (ratio ~0.5): The cohort wave passes through juvenile sizes rapidly (fish grow quickly at small sizes relative to the cycle period). Between waves, these size classes are nearly empty. The long gaps dominate the time-average.
Mild excess at large\(w\) (ratio ~1.5–1.6): Fish slow down as they approach maximum size \(w_\text{max}\). The wave bunches up there, dwelling longer at large sizes than at intermediate sizes. This raises the time-average above the fixed-point level.

The total ~1.23× biomass advantage (at λ=2.0) is a biomass-weighted integral of these effects. Large fish dominate biomass (each individual contributes proportionally more at high \(w\)), so the ~1.5× elevation at large sizes drives most of the integrated gain. The 2.5× excess recruits contribute little to total biomass because \(w \cdot \Delta w\) is tiny at the smallest sizes.
The knife-edge gear in the fishing experiments above selects fish at \(w \geq w_\text{mat} = 10\text{g}\), which sits squarely in the “~1.5× elevated” region. The limit cycle does make large adults more available on average than the fixed point and that elevated availability contributes most of the ~1.23× total biomass advantage. The 2.5× surplus recruits cannot be harvested before maturation, and the depleted intermediate size classes represent a growth bottleneck limiting how much of that recruitment reaches harvestable size during each cycle.

title: Day 16: The Unstable Fixed Point, the Limit-Cycle Advantage, and What Fishing Does to It
section: Does Constant Fishing Affect the Limit Cycle?
text:
Does Constant Fishing Affect the Limit Cycle?
With the ratio characterised and understood, the next question is what happens when you fish the system. The limit-cycle advantage is real ~13% above the fixed-point biomass at λ=2.05 but it could be fragile. The intuition is that adding fishing mortality partially compensates the supercritical resource condition that drives the Hopf bifurcation: if fishing tips the system back below the bifurcation point, the limit cycle should disappear and the fixed point re-stabilise.
The test: scan effort levels from 0 to 0.5 with knife-edge selectivity at \(w_\text{mat}\), using the confirmed working setup (predictor-corrector, t_save = 0.2, limit-cycle initial condition).


Code
test_constant_fishing <- function(effort, lambda = 2.05, t_total = 600) {
  p  <- make_params(lambda = lambda)
  gp <- p@gear_params
  gp$sel_func        <- "knife_edge"
  gp$knife_edge_size <- p@species_params$w_mat
  gp$catchability    <- 1
  gear_params(p)     <- gp

  p@initial_n_pp[] <- p@cc_pp * 0.1
  sim_init <- project(p, t_max = 10, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                      progress_bar = FALSE, effort = 0,
                      method = "predictor-corrector")
  idx  <- p@w >= 10 & p@w <= 100
  last <- dim(sim_init@n)[1]
  sim_init@n[last,,idx] <- sim_init@n[last,,idx] / 1e3

  sim <- project(sim_init, t_max = t_total - 10, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                 progress_bar = FALSE, effort = effort,
                 method = "predictor-corrector")
  bm <- getBiomass(sim)[, "Anchovy"]
  t  <- as.numeric(names(bm))
  list(sim = sim, bm = bm, t = t)
}

text:
What’s Next

Peak-only fishing: Does concentrating effort at biomass peaks change yield or biomass compared to spreading the same total effort evenly? The motivation has changed since constant fishing does not kill the cycle, the question is no longer about preserving the oscillation, but about whether the timing of mortality within a cycle matters at all.
Find the actual collapse threshold: At what effort does the population eventually collapse? The self-compensation mechanism keeps the mean almost constant up to effort = 0.5, but there must be a limit.
Step-by-step model building: Return to the simplified transport equation and build up mechanisms one at a time (linear model → reproduction → feedback loop → resource depletion) as outlined at the end of Days 14–15.

title: Day 18: The Limit Cycle Is a Global Attractor, but Supercritical vs Subcritical Is Still Open
text:
Day 17 identified a weakness in the initialisation procedure used throughout the preceding experiments. The two-stage perturbation in make_limit_cycle_sim, depleting the resource to destabilise the system, then knocking down mature fish by a fixed factor of 1000, was the mechanism used to kick the system off the unstable fixed point and onto the limit cycle. But this is an ad-hoc procedure. It does not tell us whether the limit cycle is a genuine attractor (i.e. trajectories from arbitrary initial conditions converge to it) or whether it is fragile, reached only by this particular path.
Day 17’s “What’s Next” proposed a direct test: vary the perturbation magnitude across a wide range and check whether all trajectories converge to the same orbit. If they do, the limit cycle is a stable attractor and its basin of attraction is at least as large as the range of perturbations tested. If they diverge, the initialisation is doing more work than assumed.
Today runs exactly that experiment.

Setup
The helper functions are carried over from previous days. The one change from Day 17 is that make_limit_cycle_sim now accepts a perturbation argument (the factor by which the mature stock is divided at \(t = 10\)) and uses the tr_bdf2 integrator for improved stability.


Code
make_params <- function(lambda = 2.05, resource_decrease = 0.001) {
  a0    <- 100
  kappa <- a0 * exp(-6.9 * (lambda - 1))
  no_w  <- round(log(66.5 / 0.0003) / 0.1)

  params <- newSingleSpeciesParams(
    species_name = "Anchovy",
    w_min = 0.0003, w_max = 66.5, w_mat = 10,
    no_w = no_w, lambda = lambda, kappa = kappa,
    alpha = 0.1, gamma = 750, ks = 0
  )
  r      <- getResourceRate(params) * resource_decrease
  params <- setResource(params, resource_rate = r,
                        resource_dynamics = "resource_semichemostat")
  params
}

make_limit_cycle_sim <- function(params, t_total = 600, effort = 0, perturbation = 1e-3) {
  params@initial_n_pp[] <- params@cc_pp * 0.1

  sim_init <- project(params, t_max = 10, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
                      progress_bar = FALSE, effort = 0,
                      method = "tr_bdf2")
  idx  <- params@w >= 10 & params@w <= 100
  last <- dim(sim_init@n)[1]
  sim_init@n[last, , idx] <- sim_init@n[last, , idx] / perturbation

  project(sim_init, t_max = t_total - 10, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.2,
          progress_bar = FALSE, effort = effort,
          method = "tr_bdf2")
}

test_perturbation <- function(perturbation, lambda = 2.05, t_total = 600) {
  p   <- make_params(lambda = lambda)
  sim <- make_limit_cycle_sim(p, t_total = t_total, perturbation = perturbation)
  bm  <- getBiomass(sim)[, "Anchovy"]
  t   <- as.numeric(names(bm))
  list(sim = sim, bm = bm, t = t)
}

Experiment: Varying the Perturbation Magnitude
Five perturbation levels are tested: 1, 5, 10, 100, and 1000. A perturbation of 1000 means the mature stock (\(w \geq w_\text{mat}\)) is divided by 1000 at \(t = 10\), leaving it at 0.1% of its value just before the knock-down. A perturbation of 1 means no knock-down is applied at all as the system evolves from the depleted-resource initial condition alone.


Code
perturbation    <- c(1e3, 1e2, 1e1, 5, 1)
results_fishing <- lapply(perturbation, test_perturbation)

title: Day 18: The Limit Cycle Is a Global Attractor, but Supercritical vs Subcritical Is Still Open
text:
What the Plot Shows
The five trajectories are essentially indistinguishable after \(t = 550\). They share the same amplitude (oscillating between roughly \(0.03\) and \(0.16\)), the same period (approximately 7–8 years), and the same waveform shape. The only visible residual difference is a slight phase offset between some lines, most visible around the peaks near \(t \approx 570\)–\(575\), but even this appears to be shrinking over the interval shown.
This is direct evidence for two properties of the system:
The fixed point is unstable: None of the trajectories converge to a constant biomass. Every initial condition, including the case with no knock-down (Perturbation = 1), evolves into sustained oscillation. The fixed point is present in the dynamics (the trajectories oscillate around it) but it does not attract any of the tested initial conditions.
The limit cycle is a stable attractor: All five trajectories, starting from initial conditions that differ by three orders of magnitude in the mature stock, converge to the same periodic orbit. This is the defining property of a stable (attracting) limit cycle: it draws in trajectories from its neighbourhood and, as the experiment shows, from a very wide neighbourhood. The basin of attraction extends at least from Perturbation = 1 to Perturbation = 1000, which covers the full range of plausible starting states for this system.
The basin of attraction is large: Perturbation = 1000 corresponds to reducing the adult stock to 0.1% of its value which is an extreme disturbance that would, in a stable-equilibrium system, either drive the population to extinction or require a very long recovery transient. Here it does neither: the system returns to the same orbit on a timescale comparable to the perturbation = 1 case. The cohort-wave mechanism is robust enough to self-organise from a near-empty adult population.

title: Day 18: The Limit Cycle Is a Global Attractor, but Supercritical vs Subcritical Is Still Open
section: What This Means for the Initialisation Procedure
text:
What This Means for the Initialisation Procedure
The experiment also validates the two-stage initialisation used throughout Days 10–17. The specific choice of dividing the mature stock by 1000 was arbitrary; the results here confirm that essentially any perturbation large enough to break the system away from the vicinity of the fixed point produces the same long-run behaviour. The initialisation procedure is not injecting a particular orbit; it is simply providing a push that allows the natural attractor to assert itself.

title: Day 18: The Limit Cycle Is a Global Attractor, but Supercritical vs Subcritical Is Still Open
section: Hysteresis Test: Is the Bifurcation Subcritical or Supercritical?
text:
Hysteresis Test: Is the Bifurcation Subcritical or Supercritical?
Day 17 proposed a second diagnostic: sweep the resource_decrease parameter forward (stable → oscillating) and then backward (oscillating → stable), carrying the final state of each run into the next. If the system shows hysteresis, the limit cycle persisting at lower resource_decrease on the way back than where it appeared on the way forward,then that is evidence of a subcritical Hopf bifurcation, with a bistable region where both the fixed point and the limit cycle are stable simultaneously. If the two sweeps coincide, the bifurcation is supercritical.
Mizer includes a diffusion term arising from variability in prey sizes (the jump-growth equation). Before attempting to switch it off, it is worth checking whether it is actually non-zero for this parameterisation.


Code
p_check <- make_params(lambda = 2.05)
range(getDiffusion(p_check))


[1] 0 0


getDiffusion returns zero across all size classes. The diffusion term is already zero for this single-species anchovy parameterisation and the jump-growth diffusion evaluates to zero because the effective variance in prey sizes collapses to zero under this resource and feeding-kernel setup. No special handling is needed; make_params is used directly and the model is already in the pure advection-mortality regime.
The sweep helper runs each resource_decrease value for 300 years, uses the last 40% of each run to estimate oscillation amplitude, and passes the final state directly into the next run’s initial condition.


Code
run_rd_sweep <- function(rd_seq, init_n = NULL, init_n_pp = NULL,
                         t_run = 300, lambda = 2.05, label = "") {
  out       <- data.frame(rd = rd_seq, amp = NA_real_, bm_mean = NA_real_)
  state_n   <- init_n
  state_npp <- init_n_pp

  for (i in seq_along(rd_seq)) {
    p <- make_params(lambda = lambda, resource_decrease = rd_seq[i])
    if (!is.null(state_n)) {
      p@initial_n[]    <- state_n
      p@initial_n_pp[] <- state_npp
    }
    sim <- project(p, t_max = t_run, dt = 0.1, t_save = 0.5,
                   progress_bar = FALSE, effort = 0, method = "tr_bdf2")
    bm   <- getBiomass(sim)[, "Anchovy"]
    tv   <- as.numeric(names(bm))
    late <- bm[tv > t_run * 0.6]
    last <- dim(sim@n)[1]

    state_n   <- sim@n[last, , ]
    state_npp <- sim@n_pp[last, ]

    out$amp[i]     <- max(late) - min(late)
    out$bm_mean[i] <- mean(late)
  }
  list(df = out, n_final = state_n, npp_final = state_npp)
}

rd_seq <- seq(0.001, 0.01, length.out = 10)

fwd <- run_rd_sweep(rd_seq, label = "FWD")
bwd <- run_rd_sweep(rev(rd_seq),
                    init_n    = fwd$n_final,
                    init_n_pp = fwd$npp_final,
                    label     = "BWD")




Code
fwd_df <- fwd$df
bwd_df <- bwd$df[order(bwd$df$rd), ]

thresh     <- 0.005
fwd_onset  <- fwd_df$rd[which(fwd_df$amp  > thresh)[1]]
bwd_offset <- bwd_df$rd[tail(which(bwd_df$amp > thresh), 1)]

plot(fwd_df$rd, fwd_df$amp,
     type = "l", col = "steelblue", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "resource_decrease",
     ylab = "Oscillation amplitude (max − min biomass)",
     main = "Hysteresis test",
     ylim = c(0, max(fwd_df$amp, bwd_df$amp) * 1.1))
lines(bwd_df$rd, bwd_df$amp, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
abline(v = fwd_onset,  lty = 2, col = "steelblue")
abline(v = bwd_offset, lty = 2, col = "firebrick")
legend("topleft",
       legend = c(
         sprintf("Forward  — onset  rd ≈ %.4f", fwd_onset),
         sprintf("Backward — offset rd ≈ %.4f", bwd_offset)
       ),
       col = c("steelblue", "firebrick"), lwd = 2)

title: Day 18: The Limit Cycle Is a Global Attractor, but Supercritical vs Subcritical Is Still Open
text:
What the Hysteresis Plot Shows
The forward and backward curves both drop toward zero amplitude in roughly the same region, and neither jumps discontinuously — encouraging signs for a supercritical bifurcation. But they don’t fully coincide either. The backward curve keeps oscillating down to \(\text{rd} \approx 0.008\), while the forward curve’s amplitude has already fallen toward the noise floor well before that point. Read at face value, that gap is exactly what a subcritical bifurcation with a small bistability window would look like: the limit cycle outliving its own forward onset on the way back down.
The obvious objection is that the forward “onset” detector is contaminated: it’s flagged at rd = 0.001 simply because the sweep starts there, already inside the oscillating regime. That’s true, but it only explains away half the gap — it means the forward transition point isn’t well measured by fwd_onset, not that the gap itself isn’t real. The backward offset at \(\text{rd} \approx 0.008\) is a direct, uncontaminated measurement, and the forward curve’s amplitude is visibly near zero below that value on the plot. Critical slowing down near the bifurcation is a real confound too: a 300-year run may not fully settle before the next step is taken, which would inflate the backward curve’s apparent transition point without any true hysteresis behind it. But at this sweep resolution and run length, that explanation can’t be distinguished from genuine bistability.
So the two signatures don’t agree. Continuous, square-root-like amplitude growth on the forward sweep (\(A \propto \sqrt{|r - r_c|}\), no discontinuous jump) is a supercritical signature. The unresolved gap between the forward and backward transition points is what a subcritical bifurcation with a bistable window would produce. Given that, this data can’t yet confirm the bifurcation is supercritical. It may be subcritical with a narrow bistable region that a coarse 10-point sweep and 300-year runs aren’t resolving cleanly, or it may be supercritical with the whole gap explained by critical slowing down. Distinguishing the two needs either much longer per-step runs (to let slow convergence fully resolve) or a finer rd grid around 0.008 to see whether the gap holds up or recedes. That’s left open rather than settled here.
The effort scans in Days 16–17 are sometimes read as a second confirmation of the same picture: the transition back to a stable fixed point at high fishing effort also showed damped spiralling rather than a discontinuous jump. But calling that “consistent with supercritical” is a weaker claim than it sounds, and it’s now doubly so given the hysteresis gap above. The spiral there persists for a good number of cycles before settling, longer than critical slowing down alone would predict, and it isn’t a numerical-integration artefact either, since the same solver and timestep produce clean, non-decaying oscillation everywhere else in this post. Asserting consistency glosses over that persistence rather than explaining it. Rather than a blanket statement, this needs a closer look: plotting the maximum and minimum of each cycle separately as effort increases (see What’s Next) rather than the collapsed max − min amplitude used so far.

title: Day 18: The Limit Cycle Is a Global Attractor, but Supercritical vs Subcritical Is Still Open
text:
What’s Next

Try a different perturbation type to see whether the same convergence-to-attractor result holds no matter what form the perturbation takes, rather than relying solely on the mature-stock knock-down used so far.
Run with balance = FALSE in setResource. The effects should be more realistic, since the model is not inflating some rates to compensate for others.
Plot maximum and minimum separately instead of plotting max − min, to get a bifurcation-diagram look at the amplitude data rather than a single collapsed amplitude curve.
Resolve whether the forward/backward gap at rd ≈ 0.008 is real hysteresis or a run-length artefact. Rerun the sweep with much longer per-step runs (to let critical slowing down fully settle) and a finer resource_decrease grid around 0.008, since the current 10-point, 300-year sweep can’t distinguish a genuinely subcritical bifurcation with a narrow bistable window from a supercritical one confounded by slow convergence.
